content: Immersion in water during labor and birth has gained popularity and is widely accepted in many countries, particularly in midwifery-led care settings. However, concerns remain regarding potential risks such as neonatal water inhalation, increased admissions to neonatal intensive care units (NICU), maternal or neonatal infections, and obstetric anal sphincter injuries (OASIS). This review aimed to evaluate the effects of water immersion during the first, second, and third stages of labor on maternal and neonatal outcomes. The review included 15 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted between 1990 and 2015, involving a total of 3,663 women. These trials primarily took place in hospital labor wards, with varying levels of routine medical intervention. None of the studies were conducted in midwifery-led care settings. Most trials did not specify the parity of participants, and the studies were subject to varying degrees of bias due to the inability to blind the intervention and insufficient information about randomization methods. Immersion in Water During the First Stage of Labor: Mode of Birth: There is likely little or no difference in the rate of spontaneous vaginal births between women who used water immersion and those who did not (83% vs. 82%; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in instrumental vaginal births (12% vs. 14%; low-quality evidence) or cesarean sections (5% vs. 4%; low-quality evidence). Perineal Trauma: There is insufficient evidence to determine the effect of water immersion on thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears (3% vs. 3%; moderate-quality evidence). Blood Loss: The evidence is very limited and does not show a clear effect on estimated blood loss (very low-quality evidence). Pain Management: Women who used water immersion were slightly less likely to require regional analgesia, with a reduction from 43% to 39% (moderate-quality evidence). Neonatal Outcomes: There is insufficient evidence to determine the impact of water immersion on NICU admissions (6% vs. 6%; low-quality evidence) or neonatal infection rates (1% vs. 1%; very low-quality evidence). Perinatal deaths were not reported in the included trials. Immersion in Water During the Second Stage of Labor: Mode of Birth: There were no clear differences between groups in rates of spontaneous vaginal births (98% vs. 97%; low-quality evidence), instrumental vaginal births (2% vs. 2%; very low-quality evidence), or cesarean sections (0% vs. 2%; very low-quality evidence). Neonatal Outcomes: NICU admission rates were similar between groups (8% vs. 11%; very low-quality evidence). Neonatal infection rates were not reported, but one trial noted no significant differences in neonatal temperatures at birth or fever during the first week of life (very low-quality evidence). One perinatal death occurred in the water immersion group, attributed to intrauterine infection in a mother with HIV (very low-quality evidence). Other Outcomes: Thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears and estimated blood loss were not reported for this stage of labor. The use of regional analgesia was not relevant to the second stage. Early vs. Late Entry into Water: Only one trial compared early versus late entry into the water during the first stage of labor, involving 200 women. The data were insufficient to draw any clear conclusions about differences in outcomes. Authors' Conclusions: For healthy women at low risk of complications, moderateto low-quality evidence suggests that water immersion during the first stage of labor likely has little effect on the mode of birth or perineal trauma but may reduce the use of regional analgesia. Evidence for water immersion during the second stage of labor is limited and does not show clear differences in maternal or neonatal outcomes. There is no evidence of increased adverse effects to the fetus, neonate, or mother from laboring or giving birth in water. However, the available evidence is limited by clinical variability and heterogeneity across trials, and no studies have been conducted in midwifery-led care settings.
